questions.stem: What does the change in breathing rate equal?

options.text: The mean of the two rates
options.explanation: The mean hides the change instead of measuring it.

questions.stem: Why must every participant perform the same exercise?

options.explanation: Safety is not the comparison reason.
Counting works at any rhythm.
Practicality is not the scientific reason.

options.text: So the change in breathing rate is comparable across participants
options.explanation: Identical demand makes the counts comparable.

questions.stem: Which conclusion follows from the change in breathing rate?

options.text: Exercise makes breathing both faster and deeper
options.explanation: Both the count per minute and the breath size rise.
The counts rise after exercise.
The change is the whole point of the practical.

options.text: Exercise only deepens breathing, not its rate
options.explanation: Both frequency and depth increase.

questions.stem: State the equation for the change in breathing rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Change in breathing rate equals the rate after exercise minus the rate at rest.

questions.stem: Name two variables that must be kept the same across participants.
questions.modelAnswer: The type and duration of exercise, and the environment such as temperature, plus the same counting method.

questions.stem: Explain why the mean of several participants is better than one person's numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: Because individuals differ in fitness, motivation and health, so one person's counts could be atypical; averaging across the group smooths those quirks and gives a value that reflects the exercise effect rather than one body's idiosyncrasies.

questions.stem: A student counts 14 breaths per minute at rest and 30 straight after one minute of step-ups. State the change and the biological cause.
questions.modelAnswer: The change is 16 breaths per minute; the cause is the muscles' extra oxygen demand and extra carbon dioxide output during the step-ups, which drove the deeper, faster breathing.

questions.stem: Which fix addresses uneven exercise intensity?

options.explanation: More data does not standardise effort.

options.text: A controlled exercise such as step-ups at a set pace
options.explanation: Standardising the effort removes the variability.

Age is not the intensity fix.

questions.stem: Why is breathing rate hard to measure accurately?

options.explanation: Cooperation is not the stated problem.

options.text: It changes quickly after exercise, so timing errors distort the count
options.explanation: The rate decays while you count it.

questions.stem: Why might two participants show different changes despite identical exercise?

options.explanation: No stopwatch is involved in breath counting.

options.text: Fitness, motivation and health differ between people
options.explanation: Individual physiology colours the response.
They can, imperfectly.

options.text: Because exercise always gives the same change
options.explanation: It does not; variation is the norm.

questions.stem: State the solution for the timing error in breath counting.
questions.modelAnswer: Begin counting immediately after exercise and count for a fixed short period, such as fifteen seconds, then multiply up to a per-minute rate.

questions.stem: Name three external conditions that can influence breathing rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature, air quality and stress levels.

questions.stem: Explain why a step-up test at a fixed pace is fairer than 'run as fast as you can'.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a fixed pace gives every participant the same workload, so any difference in the breathing response reflects the person, not a private choice of effort; 'as fast as you can' lets motivation and ability silently rewrite the intensity.

questions.stem: Design the control that would let a class compare smokers and non-smokers on this practical, naming one extra limitation it introduces.
questions.modelAnswer: Match participants for age and fitness across both groups, hold the exercise and environment identical, and compare the mean changes; the extra limitation is that smoking history varies in amount and duration, so the groups are not perfectly matched even after controls.
